questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.11
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
Which functions does NOT implement the Karnaugh map given below?

                                        

  1. $(w + x) y$
  2. $xy + yw$
  3. $(w + x) (\bar{w} + y) (\bar{x} + y)$
  4. None of the above

review.concept: Digital Logic - Karnaugh Map Implicants and Boolean Function Equivalence
review.notes: All three algebraic expressions A, B, and C simplify to (w+x)y, which perfectly covers the K-map minterms and respects don't-cares. Hence, none fail to implement the map. Official key D verified.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.12
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
The following arrangement of master-slave flip flops

has the initial state of $P, Q$ as $0, 1$ (respectively). After three clock cycles the output state $P, Q$ is (respectively),

  1. $1, 0$
  2. $1, 1$
  3. $0, 0$
  4. $0, 1$

review.concept: Digital Logic - Synchronous Sequential Circuits and Flip-Flop Transitions
review.notes: Synchronous JK-D state progression from (0,1): cycle 1 gives (1,0), cycle 2 gives (0,1), cycle 3 gives (1,0). Matches official key A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.13
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.questionHtml:
A graphics card has on board memory of 1 MB. Which of the following modes can the card not support?

  1. 1600 x 400 resolution with 256 colors on a 17 inch monitor
  2. 1600 x 400 resolution with 16 million colors on a 14 inch monitor
  3. 800 x 400 resolution with 16 million colors on a 17 inch monitor
  4. 800 x 800 resolution with 256 colors on a 14 inch monitor

review.concept: Operating Systems / Computer Graphics - Frame Buffer Memory Sizing
review.notes: Mode B requires 1600 * 400 * 3 = 1.92 MB, exceeding the 1 MB on-board graphics memory. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.14
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the values of $A = 2.0 \times 10^{30}, B = -2.0 \times 10^{30}, C = 1.0,$ and the sequence 

   X:= A + B          Y:= A + C   
   X:= X + C          Y:= Y + B

executed on a computer where floating point numbers are represented with $32$ bits. The values for $X$ and $Y$ will be

  1. $X = 1.0, Y = 1.0$
  2. $X = 1.0, Y = 0.0$
  3. $X = 0.0, Y = 1.0$
  4. $X = 0.0, Y = 0.0$

review.concept: Computer Arithmetic - IEEE 754 Floating-Point Precision Loss and Alignment
review.notes: Due to finite 24-bit mantissa precision, A+C loses C completely (swamping), making Y become 0.0 after adding B, whereas X computes A+B=0 first then adds C=1.0. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.15
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose you are given an array $s[1....n]$ and a procedure reverse $(s, i, j)$ which reverses the order of elements in $s$ between positions $i$ and $j$ (both inclusive). What does the following sequence do, where $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$:

           reverse (s, 1, k);
           reverse (s, k+1, n);
           reverse (s, 1, n);
  1. Rotates $s$ left by $k$ positions
  2. Leaves $s$ unchanged 
  3. Reverses all elements of $s$
  4. None of the above

review.concept: Algorithms - Array Reversal Algorithm for Block Rotation
review.notes: Three-step reversal (A^R B^R)^R = BA rotates the array left by k positions. Matches official key A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.16
questions.subject: Programming and DS
questions.questionHtml:
Let LASTPOST, LASTIN and LASTPRE denote the last vertex visited `in a postorder, inorder and preorder traversal respectively, of a complete binary tree. Which of the following is always true?

  1. LASTIN = LASTPOST
  2. LASTIN = LASTPRE
  3. LASTPRE = LASTPOST
  4. None of the above

review.concept: Programming and Data Structures - Binary Tree Traversal Invariants
review.notes: In a complete binary tree, LASTPOST is always the root, while LASTIN and LASTPRE depend on leaf placements and differ in general (e.g. n=2 or n=6). Hence none of the equations hold universally. Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.17
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the following functions

  • $f(n) = 3n^{\sqrt{n}}$
  • $g(n) = 2^{\sqrt{n}{\log_{2}n}}$
  • $h(n) = n!$

Which of the following is true?

  1. $h(n)$ is $O(f(n))$
  2. $h(n)$ is $O(g(n))$
  3. $g(n)$ is not $O(f(n))$
  4. $f(n)$ is $O(g(n))$

review.concept: Algorithms - Asymptotic Growth Rates and Factorial Comparison
review.notes: g(n) = 2^(sqrt(n) log n) = n^sqrt(n), so f(n) = 3*g(n) is strictly O(g(n)). Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.18
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
Let $G$ be an undirected connected graph with distinct edge weights. Let $e_{max}$ be the edge with maximum weight and $e_{min}$ the edge with minimum weight. Which of the following statements is false?

  1. Every minimum spanning tree of $G$ must contain $e_{min}$
  2. If $e_{max}$ is in a minimum spanning tree, then its removal must disconnect $G$
  3. No minimum spanning tree contains $e_{max}$
  4. $G$ has a unique minimum spanning tree

review.concept: Algorithms / Graph Theory - Properties of Minimum Spanning Trees (MST)
review.notes: If G is a tree or e_max is a bridge, e_max MUST be included in the MST. Thus statement C is false. Matches official key C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.20
questions.subject: Programming in C
questions.questionHtml:
The value of $j$ at the end of the execution of the following C program:

int incr (int i)
{ 
    static int count = 0;
    count = count + i;
    return (count);
} 
main  { 
    int i, j; 
    for (i = 0; i <= 4; i++)
       j = incr (i);
}

is:

  1. $10$
  2. $4$
  3. $6$
  4. $7$

review.concept: Programming in C - Static Storage Duration and Function Scope
review.notes: Static count variable accumulates 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 across loop iterations. Matches official key A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.21, ISRO2015-24
questions.subject: Compiler Design
questions.questionHtml:
Given the following expression grammar:

$$\begin{align}
E &\to E * F \mid F + E \mid F \\[1em]
F &\to F - F \mid id
\end{align}$$

Which of the following is true?

  1. $*$ has higher precedence than $+$
  2. $-$ has higher precedence than $*$
  3. $+$ and $-$ have same precedence
  4. $+$ has higher precedence than $*$

review.concept: Compiler Design - Context-Free Grammars and Operator Precedence Hierarchy
review.notes: F derives - while E derives * and +. Non-terminals lower in the grammar hierarchy bind tighter, so - has higher precedence than *. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.22
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose the time to service a page fault is on the average $10$ milliseconds, while a memory access takes $1$ microsecond. Then a $99.99\%$ hit ratio results in average memory access time of

  1. $1.9999$ milliseconds
  2. $1$ millisecond
  3. $9.999$ microseconds
  4. $1.9999$ microseconds

review.concept: Operating Systems - Effective Memory Access Time (EMAT) and Page Fault Overhead
review.notes: EMAT = 0.9999 * 1 us + 0.0001 * 10,000 us = 1.9999 us. Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.23
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following is not a valid deadlock prevention scheme?

  1. Release all resources before requesting a new resource.
  2. Number the resources uniquely and never request a lower numbered resource than the last one requested.
  3. Never request a resource after releasing any resource.
  4. Request and all required resources be allocated before execution.

review.concept: Operating Systems - Deadlock Prevention vs Concurrency Control Schemes
review.notes: Never requesting after releasing is the 2PL shrinking phase for serializability, which does NOT prevent deadlocks (transactions under 2PL can still deadlock). Matches official key C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.24
questions.subject: Databases
questions.questionHtml:
Given the following relation instance.

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|}\hline \text{X} & \text{Y} & \text{Z} \\\hline   \text{1} & \text{4} & \text{2} \\   \text{1} & \text{5} & \text{3} \\  \text{1} & \text{6} & \text{3} \\ \text{3} & \text{2} & \text{2} \\\hline \end{array}$$

Which of the following functional dependencies are satisfied by the instance?

  1. $XY \rightarrow Z$ and $Z \rightarrow Y$
  2. $YZ \rightarrow X$ and $Y \rightarrow Z$
  3. $YZ \rightarrow X$ and $X \rightarrow Z$
  4. $XZ \rightarrow Y$ and $Y \rightarrow X$

review.concept: Databases - Functional Dependency Satisfaction in Relational Instances
review.notes: All Y values are distinct, so Y->Z and YZ->X are trivially satisfied. X->Z, Z->Y, and XZ->Y all have violations. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.25
questions.subject: Databases
questions.questionHtml:
Given relations r(w, x) and s(y, z) the result of

select distinct w, x 
from r, s 

is guaranteed to be same as r, provided.

  1. r has no duplicates and s is non-empty
  2. r and s have no duplicates
  3. s has no duplicates and r is non-empty
  4. r and s have the same number of tuples

review.concept: Databases - Relational Algebra and SQL Cartesian Product Equivalence
review.notes: Cartesian product requires non-empty s to produce tuples, and distinct requires r to have no duplicates to maintain cardinality. Matches official key A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 2.26
questions.subject: Databases
questions.questionHtml:
In SQL, relations can contain null values, and comparisons with null values are treated as unknown. Suppose all comparisons with a null value are treated as false. Which of the following pairs is not equivalent?

  1. $x=5\; not(not(x=5)) $
  2. $x=5 \; x \gt 4 \text{ and }x\lt6 $, where $x $ is an integer
  3. $x \neq 5$ not(x=5)
  4. none of the above

review.concept: Databases - SQL Three-Valued Logic and NULL Comparison Semantics
review.notes: When x is NULL, (x != 5) is false by rule, but not(x = 5) evaluates to not(false) = true. Thus pair C is not equivalent. Matches official key C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2000 | Question: 17
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
An array contains four occurrences of $0$, five occurrences of $1$, and three occurrences of $2$ in any order. The array is to be sorted using swap operations (elements that are swapped need to be adjacent).

  1.  What is the minimum number of swaps needed to sort such an array in the worst case?
  2.  Give an ordering of  elements in the above array so that the minimum number of swaps needed to sort the array is maximum.

review.concept: Algorithms - Sorting with Adjacent Swaps and Maximum Inversion Number
review.notes: Adjacent swaps equal inversion count. Worst-case array 2,2,2, 1,1,1,1,1, 0,0,0,0 has 3*5 + 3*4 + 5*4 = 15 + 12 + 20 = 47 inversions. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.4
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.questionHtml:
Consider the regular expression $(0 + 1) (0+1) \dots N$ times. The minimum state finite automaton that recognizes the language represented by this regular expression contains

  1. $n$ states
  2. $n+1$ states
  3. $n+2$ states
  4. None of the above

review.concept: Theory of Computation - Minimal Finite Automata for Fixed-Length String Languages
review.notes: Automaton recognizing strings of length exactly n requires n+1 states (q0 through qn). Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.5
questions.subject: Theory of Computation
questions.questionHtml:
Context-free languages are closed under:

  1. Union, intersection

  2. Union, Kleene closure

  3. Intersection, complement

  4. Complement, Kleene closure

review.concept: Theory of Computation - Closure Properties of Context-Free Languages (CFL)
review.notes: CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, and Kleene star, but not closed under intersection or complement. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.7
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following expressions is not equivalent to $\bar{x}$?

  1. $x \text{ NAND } x$
  2. $x \text{ NOR } x$
  3. $x \text{ NAND } 1$
  4. $x \text{ NOR } 1$

review.concept: Digital Logic - Universal Logic Gates and Inverter Realization
review.notes: x NOR 1 = not(x + 1) = not(1) = 0, which is constant 0, not x_bar. Matches official key D.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.8
questions.subject: Digital Logic
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following functions implements the Karnaugh map shown below?

  1. $\bar{A}B + CD$
  2. $D(C+A)$
  3. $AD+\bar{A}B$
  4. $(C+D) (\bar{C}+D) + (A+B)$

review.concept: Digital Logic - Karnaugh Map Minimization with Don't Care Conditions
review.notes: Grouping quad CD=11 (gives CD) and quad rows 11,10 with cols 01,11 (gives AD) yields CD + AD = D(C + A). Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.9
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.questionHtml:
Listed below are some operating system abstractions (in the left column) and the hardware components (in the right column)$$\small \begin{array}{cl|cl}\hline \text{(A)}& \text{Thread}  &  \text{1.}& \text{Interrupt} \\\hline 
\text{(B)}& \text{Virtual address space} & \text{2.}& \text{Memory} \\\hline 
\text{(C)} &\text{File system} & \text{3.} &\text{CPU} \\\hline 
\text{(D)} &\text{Signal} & \text{4.}& \text{Disk} \\\hline \end{array}$$

  1. (A) – 2 (B) – 4 (C) – 3 (D) – 1 
  2. (A) – 1 (B) – 2 (C) – 3 (D) – 4
  3. (A) – 3 (B) – 2 (C) – 4 (D) – 1
  4. (A) – 4 (B) – 1 (C) – 2 (D) – 3

review.concept: Operating Systems - Hardware Components and Operating System Abstractions
review.notes: Thread virtualizes CPU (3), Virtual address space virtualizes Memory (2), File system virtualizes Disk (4), Signal virtualizes Interrupt (1). Matches official key C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.10
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.questionHtml:
Which of the following disk scheduling strategies is likely to give the best throughput?

  1. Farthest cylinder next

  2. Nearest cylinder next

  3. First come first served

  4. Elevator algorithm

review.concept: Operating Systems - Disk Scheduling Algorithms and Throughput Optimization
review.notes: Nearest cylinder next (SSTF) minimizes average seek time per request, yielding the highest throughput. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.11, UGCNET-Dec2015-II: 44
questions.subject: Operating System
questions.questionHtml:
System calls are usually invoked by using

  1. a software interrupt
  2. polling
  3. an indirect jump
  4. a privileged instruction

review.concept: Operating Systems - System Call Invocation via Software Interrupts / Traps
review.notes: System calls are invoked via software interrupts (traps) which switch the CPU from user mode to kernel mode via the interrupt vector. Matches official key A.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.12
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
A sorting technique is called stable if

  1. it takes $O (n \log n)$ time

  2. it maintains the relative order of occurrence of non-distinct elements

  3. it uses divide and conquer paradigm

  4. it takes $O(n)$ space

review.concept: Algorithms - Definition and Properties of Stable Sorting Algorithms
review.notes: A sort is stable if it preserves the relative order of elements having identical keys. Matches official key B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 1999 | Question: 1.13
questions.subject: Algorithms
questions.questionHtml:
Suppose we want to arrange the $n$ numbers stored in any array such that all negative values occur before all positive ones. Minimum number of exchanges required in the worst case is

  1. $n-1$
  2. $n$
  3. $n+1$
  4. None of the above

review.concept: Algorithms - Array Partitioning Bounds and Minimum Exchanges
review.notes: Two-pointer swap fixes 2 misplaced elements per exchange, requiring at most floor(n/2) exchanges in the worst case, which is strictly less than n-1. Hence none of the above. Matches official key D.
